questions.question: What are SQL JOINs and when would you use INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL joins?
questions.title: SQL JOINs — INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL
questions.direct_answer: JOINs combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column. INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right (nulls where no match). RIGHT JOIN is the mirror of LEFT. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, with nulls where there's no match. In practice, you'll use INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN 95% of the time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Can you write JOINs correctly and — more importantly — choose the right type based on the business question? 'Show me all customers and their orders' vs 'Show me customers who have orders' requires different JOINs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that LEFT JOIN includes rows with no match (nulls in the right side). Also, doing a JOIN without an ON clause creates a cartesian product — millions of rows accidentally.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Draw the Venn diagram mentally and explain it. Mention performance: JOINs on indexed columns are fast, JOINs on unindexed columns can be catastrophic for large tables.

sections.title: Understanding Join Mechanics and Choosing the Right Join
sections.content:
Each join type answers a different business question, and choosing the wrong one either silently drops data or bloats results with nulls. The key is understanding how the database matches rows from the left and right tables.

**INNER JOIN** returns only rows where the join condition matches in both tables. If a customer has no orders, they are excluded entirely. Use INNER JOIN when you only want entities that have a relationship — "show me customers who have purchased something" or "list products with at least one review."

**LEFT JOIN** returns all rows from the left table, padding with NULLs when no match exists in the right table. This is the most commonly used join because it preserves the complete left-side dataset. Use LEFT JOIN when you need "all customers, including those without orders" — the NULL values in order columns tell you which customers have never purchased.

**The anti-join pattern** uses LEFT JOIN with a WHERE clause on the right table's key being NULL to find rows with no match: `SELECT c.* FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.id IS NULL` finds customers who have never ordered. This is often more readable than `NOT EXISTS` and performs identically on modern query planners.

**RIGHT JOIN** is logically identical to LEFT JOIN with the tables reversed. Most developers avoid it in favor of LEFT JOIN with the table order swapped, because reading left-to-right matches the "primary table first" mental model. There is no performance difference.

**FULL OUTER JOIN** returns all rows from both tables, with NULLs on whichever side has no match. Use it for reconciliation reports — comparing two data sources to find mismatches. For example, joining a CRM export with an invoicing system to find customers in one system but not the other.

Think of two guest lists for a party: Table A (customers) and Table B (orders). A JOIN is asking 'which guests appear on both lists, or just one?'

**INNER JOIN** — 'Show me only customers who have placed orders.'
If a customer has no orders, they don't appear. If an order has no matching customer (orphaned data), it doesn't appear. Only the overlap.

In SQL you'd select the customer name and order total from `customers` inner joined to `orders` on matching customer ids—only rows that exist in both tables show up.

**LEFT JOIN** — 'Show me ALL customers, and their orders if they have any.'
Every customer appears even if they've never ordered. For customers with no orders, the order columns show NULL. This is the most common JOIN for reports.

With a left join, the same kind of select still pairs `customers` and `orders` on id, but every customer row is kept and the order columns are null when there is no matching order.

**RIGHT JOIN** — Mirror of LEFT JOIN. All rows from the right table, matching rows from the left. Rarely used — you can always rewrite as a LEFT JOIN by swapping table positions.

**FULL OUTER JOIN** — 'Show me everything — all customers and all orders, matched where possible.'
Customers without orders get NULLs in order columns. Orders without matching customers get NULLs in customer columns. Useful for finding data mismatches.

The practical rule: **start with LEFT JOIN** when you want 'all of X and their related Y if it exists'. Use INNER JOIN when you only care about rows that have matches in both tables.

-- Sample tables:
-- customers: id, name, email
-- orders: id, customer_id, total, order_date

-- INNER JOIN: Customers who have ordered
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count, SUM(o.total) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.name;

-- LEFT JOIN: ALL customers, even those who never ordered
SELECT c.name, COALESCE(SUM(o.total), 0) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.name;

-- LEFT JOIN to find customers WITHOUT orders
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;  -- only rows where no match exists

-- FULL OUTER JOIN: Find mismatched data
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
FULL OUTER JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.id IS NULL OR o.customer_id IS NULL;

sections.title: Join Performance and Common Pitfalls
sections.content:
Understanding join behavior goes beyond syntax — production queries fail silently when join semantics are misunderstood or performance is neglected.

**Cartesian product danger.** Omitting the ON clause or using a comma-separated FROM (implicit join) produces a cross join — every row in the left table paired with every row in the right table. Two 10,000-row tables produce 100 million rows. Always verify the ON clause matches the intended relationship.

**Duplicate rows from one-to-many joins.** When joining a parent table to a child table, parent rows are duplicated for each matching child. A customer with 5 orders appears 5 times in the result. Use GROUP BY with aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM) to collapse these back to one row per parent, or use DISTINCT when you only need the parent columns.

**Index the join column.** The join condition (ON c.id = o.customer_id) performs a lookup for every row. Without an index on o.customer_id, the database does a sequential scan of the orders table for each customer — O(n×m) complexity. A B-tree index on the foreign key column turns this into O(n×log m), often reducing query time from minutes to milliseconds on large tables.

**NULL handling in joins.** NULL never equals NULL in SQL. If the join column contains NULLs, those rows are excluded from INNER JOIN results because NULL = NULL evaluates to false. LEFT JOIN preserves them on the left side but still cannot match them to the right side. Use COALESCE or IS NOT DISTINCT FROM when you need NULL-safe join behavior.

- INNER JOIN = intersection (only matching rows from both tables)
- LEFT JOIN = all from left + matching from right (NULLs where no match)
- LEFT JOIN + WHERE right.id IS NULL = find rows in left that have NO match in right (anti-join pattern)
- Always JOIN on indexed columns — joining on non-indexed columns triggers full table scans
- CROSS JOIN (or JOIN without ON) creates a cartesian product — every row × every row. Almost never what you want.

questions.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
questions.title: WHERE vs HAVING in SQL
questions.direct_answer: WHERE filters individual rows BEFORE grouping (applied to raw data). HAVING filters groups AFTER aggregation (applied to grouped results). Use WHERE to filter rows ('only orders above $50'), use HAVING to filter groups ('only customers with more than 3 orders'). WHERE cannot use aggregate functions like COUNT() or SUM(); HAVING can.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand SQL's order of execution — FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. WHERE and HAVING sit at different stages.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using HAVING when WHERE would work — HAVING on non-aggregated columns is wasteful. WHERE is faster because it filters before grouping reduces the dataset.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the execution order and why it matters for performance. WHERE reduces rows early (less work for GROUP BY), HAVING operates on already-grouped data.

sections.title: Execution Order and Performance Implications
sections.content:
The difference between WHERE and HAVING maps directly to SQL's logical execution order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Getting this wrong causes either incorrect results or unnecessary performance overhead.

**WHERE reduces data before aggregation.** When you write `WHERE status = 'ACTIVE'`, the database eliminates non-active rows before computing any aggregates. This means the GROUP BY and aggregation functions operate on a smaller dataset, which is faster. Always push filters into WHERE when the condition does not depend on an aggregate result.

**HAVING filters on aggregate results.** When you write `HAVING COUNT(*) > 5`, the database must first group all rows, compute the count for each group, and then discard groups that don't meet the threshold. This is necessarily slower than WHERE filtering because the aggregation work has already been done for the discarded groups.

```sql
-- Efficient: WHERE filters before grouping
SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date > '2024-01-01'   -- reduces rows BEFORE aggregation
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 80000;      -- filters AFTER aggregation

-- Inefficient: using HAVING for non-aggregate filter
SELECT department, AVG(salary)
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING department != 'INTERN'     -- should be WHERE, processes all rows first
```

**Common mistake: using HAVING instead of WHERE.** Developers sometimes put non-aggregate conditions in HAVING (e.g., `HAVING department = 'Engineering'`). This works syntactically but forces the database to group all departments before filtering, wasting CPU and I/O. Modern query optimizers may push such conditions down to WHERE automatically, but relying on this is fragile — write the query correctly and let the optimizer confirm your intent.

**Combining both effectively.** A typical analytics query uses WHERE to scope the time window and entity filter, then HAVING to filter aggregated metrics: "Show me active customers (WHERE) who spent more than $1,000 this quarter (HAVING)." This pattern ensures the aggregation operates on the smallest possible dataset.

Think of SQL like an assembly line with a specific order:

1. **FROM** — Bring in raw data from tables
2. **WHERE** — Filter individual rows (acts on raw, ungrouped data)
3. **GROUP BY** — Group the surviving rows
4. **HAVING** — Filter the groups (acts on aggregated results)
5. **SELECT** — Pick which columns to show
6. **ORDER BY** — Sort the final output

**WHERE** operates at step 2 — before grouping. It sees individual rows. It cannot use COUNT(), SUM(), AVG() because groups don't exist yet.

**HAVING** operates at step 4 — after grouping. It sees aggregated results. It CAN use aggregate functions because groups are already formed.

**Example:** 'Show me departments with more than 5 employees who earn above $50K.'

For example, you select department and `COUNT(*)` from employees, use `WHERE salary` greater than fifty thousand to keep only higher earners, group by department, then `HAVING COUNT(*)` greater than five so only departments with enough of those rows remain.

WHERE eliminated low earners first (reducing the dataset). Then GROUP BY grouped the remaining employees by department. Then HAVING kept only departments with more than 5 of those high earners.

-- WHERE only: Filter individual rows
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE total > 100;

-- HAVING only: Filter after grouping
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;  -- customers with 3+ orders

-- WHERE + HAVING together: Filter rows THEN filter groups
SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS total_spent
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01'  -- only 2026 orders (row filter)
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING SUM(total) > 500;          -- only big spenders (group filter)

-- WRONG: WHERE with aggregate
-- SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE COUNT(*) > 3;  -- ERROR!
-- WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so COUNT(*) doesn't exist yet.

- WHERE filters rows (before GROUP BY), HAVING filters groups (after GROUP BY)
- WHERE cannot use aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG). HAVING can.
- Use WHERE whenever possible — it reduces data early, making GROUP BY faster
- HAVING without GROUP BY works but treats the entire table as one group — rarely useful
- SQL execution order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY
